steps.say: A blow to the temple can tear the artery that runs just under the skull. The patient may talk normally for a while, then collapse quickly as blood collects outside the tough brain covering. That talking phase between the injury and the collapse is the warning sign you must never ignore.
steps.tx: Most extradural bleeds follow a tear of the **middle meningeal artery** (temple artery under the skull) where a fracture crosses the **pterion** (thin temple bone point). The classic course is a head blow with brief concussion, then a **lucid interval** (awake talking phase), then rapid deterioration as the clot expands and coma follows within hours.

steps.say: The scan of this bleed has a shape you can recognise at a glance. It bulges inward like a lens and stops at the skull seams, which tells it apart from the crescent bleed that spreads freely. That single shape difference points straight to the right diagnosis.
steps.tx: **Computed tomography** (CT head scan) shows a biconvex lens-shaped hyperdense collection that stops at cranial **suture lines** (skull seams) because the dura is tacked down there. This separates it from a subdural **crescent** (curved spread bleed) that crosses sutures freely, so shape plus suture behaviour gives the diagnosis on one scan.

vis.alt: An illustration combining an axial CT scan showing a biconvex extradural haematoma and a diagram of a skull fracture with a torn middle meningeal artery.
vis.caption: Lens-shaped extradural clot stopping at suture lines, with the torn middle meningeal artery. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Sometimes the scan shows fresh unclotted blood swirling inside the clot. That swirl means the bleeding is still active and the clot is about to grow. When you see it, the patient goes straight to the operating theatre without waiting for another scan.
steps.tx: The **swirl sign** (mixed density clot sign) of hyperdense clot mixed with hypodense unclotted blood marks **active bleeding** (ongoing vessel leak) and predicts **expansion** (clot growth). Such patients go straight to theatre without delay for further imaging, because deterioration once expansion starts is sudden and often fatal.

steps.say: Size decides the operation even when the patient still looks well. Any clot bigger than thirty cubic centimetres comes out, whatever the coma score. Beyond that volume the brain can herniate through the tentorial opening with almost no warning.
steps.tx: Foundation guidance sets a hard size rule: any extradural clot above **30 cubic cm** (thirty cubic centimetres) is evacuated whatever the consciousness score. The reason is speed: once **temporal lobe herniation** (side-lobe squeezing past the tent) begins, collapse follows within minutes, so evacuation must not wait for the score to fall.

steps.say: Small clots in awake patients can be watched, but only within strict limits. The clot must stay below thirty cubic centimetres, thinner than fifteen millimetres, with shift under five millimetres. Any drop in consciousness converts watching into surgery at once.
steps.tx: A **Glasgow Coma Scale** (consciousness score) above **8** (eight) with a clot below **30 cubic cm** (thirty cubic centimetres), thickness below **15 mm** (fifteen millimetres) and shift below **5 mm** (five millimetres) may be watched with **serial CT** (repeat head scans) and neurosurgical cover. Any score fall converts observation to surgery without further waiting.

steps.say: The operation opens the skull widely and finds the bleeding artery. The surgeon removes the clot, seals the torn vessel, and stitches the dura up to the bone so blood cannot collect there again. A small drill hole alone is only a bridge while the team arranges transfer to a neurosurgeon.
steps.tx: **Craniotomy** (skull opening operation) with clot evacuation and **middle meningeal artery** (temple artery) coagulation is the definitive operation, finished with **dural tenting** (dura-to-bone stitches) that closes the extradural space. A small **burr hole** (drill-hole drainage) only temporises in a peripheral centre before transfer for the full procedure.

vis.alt: Neuroimaging diagram comparing characteristic patterns of epidural haematoma, subdural haematoma, subarachnoid haemorrhage in basal cisterns, and an ischaemic stroke territory.
vis.caption: CT patterns guide the operation: lens-shaped extradural clot versus crescent subdural bleed. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Bleeds at the back of the head behave differently because they come from veins, not the temple artery. The posterior fossa is a tiny box, so even a small clot there can squash the fourth ventricle and block fluid flow. Symptomatic cases go to theatre even when the clot looks small.
steps.tx: **Posterior fossa** (back-of-head compartment) extradural bleeding is usually venous from a transverse or sigmoid **sinus tear** (large vein injury), not arterial. Because this small space tolerates very little extra volume, a symptomatic clot compressing the **fourth ventricle** (fluid outlet chamber; the brain has **4** (four) ventricles in all) is evacuated even when small, before obstructive hydrocephalus and coma develop.

steps.say: Children develop this bleed more easily because their dura peels off the skull with little force and their thin skull cracks readily. After even a minor knock, a growing scalp swelling with pale skin and a falling blood count should prompt an urgent scan rather than reassurance.
steps.tx: In children the dura peels away with little force and the thin skull cracks readily, so even minor knocks can raise a paediatric extradural haematoma. A **scalp haematoma** (head swelling) plus new pallor and falling haemoglobin after a small injury needs an immediate CT, because children can slide from talking to coma very quickly.
